0.0.n: Usually placed before a noun, まさかの is used playfully here to introduce a surprising outcome.

0.1.m: ended up getting the same thing
0.1.n: かぶる means overlap here; ちゃいました is a polite past ending suggesting something happened unexpectedly.

0.3.n: 笑 in parentheses marks laughter in writing rather than a spoken word.

1.0.n: Refers to the drink near the speaker.

1.1.n: Marks this drink as what the speaker is talking about.

1.2.n: Names the powdered green tea flavor of the drink.

1.3.n: A brand name for a blended drink, written in katakana.

1.4.n: Politely finishes the statement identifying the drink.

2.0.n: The speaker uses 私 to refer to themself.

2.1.n: Marks the speaker as the topic, setting up their own drink customization.

2.2.n: Short for チョコレート; combines with チップ to name the topping.

2.3.n: Combines with チョコ to mean chocolate chips; Japanese does not mark plural here.

2.4.n: Marks the chocolate chips as what the speaker added.

2.5.n: 追加する means to add; しました makes it polite and past tense.

3.0.n: Refers to the person describing their customization.

3.1.n: Marks the speaker as the topic, contrasting their choice with the previous speaker’s.

3.2.n: A katakana menu expression for extra powder; the drink context tells us it is matcha.

3.3.n: Marks the extra-powder option as what the speaker customized.

3.4.n: Combines with する to describe changing a drink order to suit personal preferences.

3.5.n: Polite past form of する; with カスタム, it means the speaker customized the order.

4.0.n: The base of いただく used before ます; the full expression is said before eating or drinking.

4.1.n: This is only the start of ます, not a separate word.

4.2.n: Stretches the preceding sound to give the expression a cheerful, drawn-out delivery.

4.3.n: Completes ます; this subtitle split does not represent a separate word.

5.0.n: This is the opening of おいしい, not an independent word here.

5.1.n: Completes the shortened exclamation おいしっ; っ shows an abrupt stop instead of the usual final い.

6.0.n: Read おいしい; this adjective can stand alone as a casual reaction to the drink.

7.0.n: Describes the weather or surrounding air, not the temperature of the drink.

7.1.n: Follows 暑い to form 暑いとき, describing a time when the weather is hot.

7.2.n: Marks hot-weather occasions as the situation being discussed.

7.3.n: A casual intensifier common in conversation, especially associated with Kansai speech.

7.4.n: Describes how good the drink tastes; めっちゃ strengthens the reaction.

8.0.n: A casual expression of agreement, less formal than はい.

0.tip: かぶる can mean people choosing the same thing, not just physically overlapping.

1.lit: This, as for, matcha Frappuccino is.
1.tip: これは introduces what you are identifying, and です finishes the identification politely.

2.lit: I, as for, chocolate chips added.
2.tip: を marks the thing added, while しました shows the action is completed and politely stated.

3.lit: I, as for, extra powder customized.
3.tip: カスタムする is used casually for tailoring a drink order to your preferences.

4.tip: いただきます is the customary expression before eating or drinking, not a literal invitation to drink together.

5.tip: おいしっ is a clipped, spontaneous version of おいしい, expressing an immediate reaction.

6.tip: Japanese often leaves out it is when an adjective alone makes the meaning clear.

7.lit: Hot times, as for, really delicious.
7.tip: 暑い refers to hot weather; 熱い is used for something hot to the touch.

8.tip: うん is a relaxed way to agree with someone you are speaking casually with.
